sentenceSets.sentence: He was penitent in public and returned to the same behavior in private, which eventually became the more significant part of the story.

answerChoices.reasoning: An apology is a form of words offered to other people, but the sentence sets his public showing against the private return to the conduct itself, which points to an inward state he only claimed to have.
Someone chastened has been sobered by a rebuke into changing course, and this man goes straight back to the same behavior as soon as no one is watching.
Abject describes a person reduced to grovelling, whereas what the sentence shows in public is a controlled and evidently effective performance.
Humility is a general lowliness of bearing, but the sentence pairs his display with a specific wrong he went on repeating, which calls for something addressed to that wrong.
Candor would mean he told the truth about himself, which the private continuation of the behavior makes impossible.
Deference is submission to other people's standing and has nothing to do with the behavior he resumed in private.
Somberness is only a grave mood, which would not be worth contrasting with what he did when unobserved.
Evasiveness would mean he dodged the subject in public, yet the sentence presents his public conduct as the very thing that persuaded people.
Defiance in public would have given the story away at once instead of making the private relapse the surprise.
Openly refusing to be sorry would collapse the contrast the sentence builds between the public man and the private one.
Celebration in public would make no sense as a prelude to a story about relapse and hypocrisy.

sentenceSets.sentence: The pilgrims climbed the last mile of the road on their knees, penitent and silent, as their grandparents had done before them.

answerChoices.reasoning: Devoutness is steady ordinary piety, which would not require anyone to cross the final mile on their knees; the detail points to something harder than routine observance.
Reverence is awe before what is holy, and awe can be felt standing upright; the sentence supplies a deliberately painful posture that asks to be explained.
Austerity describes a plain manner of living over time, while this is one ritual act performed on one road, repeating what a previous generation did.
Asceticism is a whole life of renunciation, and the sentence confines the hardship to the last mile of a single journey.
Weariness would be an effect of the climb rather than the reason for choosing to make it on their knees.
Going unshod is another detail of the scene rather than the state of mind the sentence pairs with their silence.
Resolve explains how they endured the mile but not why the tradition demands it be crossed on the knees at all.
Exaltation is a lifting up of spirit, which sits awkwardly with people lowering themselves to the ground for the final stretch.
Boasting cannot be reconciled with pilgrims who make the climb in silence.
Disrespect would be a strange motive for crawling the last mile of a pilgrimage road.
A festive mood is contradicted by the silence the sentence explicitly attributes to them.

sentenceSets.sentence: The sentencing judge was visibly unmoved by a defendant who began to look penitent only after the verdict had been read aloud.

answerChoices.reasoning: Looking crestfallen is what losing produces in anyone, so it would be fully explained by the verdict and would give the judge nothing to be unmoved by.
Subdued names only a drop in energy, which a guilty verdict would cause in any defendant and which no judge would expect to find persuasive either way.
Cooperation is conduct through the proceedings, but the sentence fixes precisely on an appearance that arrived after the verdict rather than on how he behaved during the trial.
Sincerity would require some claim of his for the judge to weigh, and the sentence reports no statement at all, only a look adopted at a suspiciously convenient moment.
Anxiety before sentencing is ordinary self-interest and would not be the sort of display a judge could be unmoved by in the moral sense the timing implies.
Bewilderment suggests he did not understand what happened, whereas the point is that he understood the verdict very well and changed his face accordingly.
Respect toward the court is a matter of bearing throughout, not something whose arrival after the verdict would carry any particular sting.
Indignation would be a protest against the verdict, which gives the judge something to reject but not the specific hollowness the timing suggests.
Self-satisfaction after a conviction would be baffling, and the judge's reaction implies a display meant to soften him.
Triumph makes no sense from a defendant who has just heard a verdict go against him.
Shamelessness would be on view from the start rather than appearing for the first time once the verdict was read.
